Findings of Fact
1. The Commissioner of the IDEM issued an Order to Compel Response Ac(cid:415)on
(“Commissioner’s Order”) related to a 1978 spill of perchloroethylene (“PCE”), and the
resul(cid:415)ng contamina(cid:415)on of an industrial manufacturing site located at 914 Broadway
Street, Chesterton, Porter County, Indiana (“Site”) on December 13, 2019.2
2. The Commissioner’s Order was issued pursuant Ind. Code § 13-25-4-9 and sought to
“compel the implementa(cid:415)on of appropriate response ac(cid:415)vi(cid:415)es in regard to past and
ongoing releases of hazardous substances at the Site.”
3. The Commissioner’s Order was issued to the former owner of the Site - Dynamic Alliance,
Inc. - and the current owner - NIM.
4. NIM (cid:415)mely sought administra(cid:415)ve review of the Commissioner’s Order by filing its Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on
on December 31, 2019.
1 On July 1, 2024, following the enactment of House Bill 1003, the OEA was eliminated and all proceedings under its
jurisdic(cid:415)on were transferred to the Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings.
2 VCF No. 82879333.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-1912-000556
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 3 of 8
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689
2025 OALP 065, page 068

Conclusions of Law
1. This proceeding is properly before the OALP on remand pursuant to Indiana Code § 4-21.5.
2. OALP has jurisdic(cid:415)on over both the subject proceeding and the par(cid:415)es to this ac(cid:415)on and is
the ul(cid:415)mate authority. Ind. Code § 4-21.5-4; Ind. Code §§ 4-15-10.5-12 and 13.
3. The party challenging the agency’s ac(cid:415)on has the burden of proof by a preponderance of the
evidence. IC 4-21.5-3-27.5(a)(1).
4. “With respect to a(cid:425)orney fees, Indiana generally adheres to the American rule whereby each
party bears its own a(cid:425)orney fees absent an agreement between the par(cid:415)es, a statute, or
other rule to the contrary.” Song v. Iatarola, 76 N.E.3d 926, 938 (Ind. Ct. App. 2017), reh'g
granted on other grounds, 83 N.E.3d 80 (Ind. Ct. App. 2017), trans. denied.
5. At the (cid:415)me this proceeding was commenced, there was no statute or rule that would
authorize an ALJ to award a party reasonable a(cid:425)orney’s fees in an adjudica(cid:415)ve proceeding
under AOPA in devia(cid:415)on of the American rule. See, e.g., Heller Development, 2008 OEA 57
("OEA has not been authorized by the legislature to impose legal fees .... ").
6. However, in 2021 the Indiana legislature added a new sec(cid:415)on to AOPA - Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-
27.5 - which authorized an administra(cid:415)ve law judge to order an agency to pay reasonable
a(cid:425)orney fees to a party challenging an agency ac(cid:415)on if it could demonstrate that the ac(cid:415)on
was frivolous, groundless, or pursued in bad faith. Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5.
7. In its originally enacted form, Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 read:
In a proceeding under this chapter concerning an agency ac(cid:415)on, the administra(cid:415)ve
law judge shall order the agency to pay the reasonable a(cid:425)orney's fees incurred in
the proceeding by the party challenging the agency ac(cid:415)on if the party challenging
the agency ac(cid:415)on proves, by a preponderance of the evidence, that: (1) the
agency's ac(cid:415)on was frivolous or groundless; or (2) the agency pursued the ac(cid:415)on
in bad faith.
This new sec(cid:415)on of AOPA became effec(cid:415)ve on the date of its enactment - July 1, 2021.
8. The Indiana legislature amended Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 in 2023. The 2023 amendments
added a requirement to the exis(cid:415)ng statutory framework that the party seeking reasonable
a(cid:425)orney’s fee must be the “prevailing party”. See Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 (2023). The 2023
amendments also added two new grounds for an award of reasonable a(cid:425)orney’s fees if said
prevailing party could prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the agency ac(cid:415)on at
issue was based on an invalid rule or the agency failed to demonstrate that it acted within its
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-1912-000556
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 4 of 8
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689
2025 OALP 065, page 069

legal authority. See Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 (2) and (3) (2023). The 2023 amendments took
effect on July 1, 2023.
9. In conjunc(cid:415)on with the 2023 amendments to Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5, the Indiana
legislature enacted Ind. Code § 4-21.5-2-8 which states that the “amendments made to IC 4-
21.5-3-27.5… in the 2023 session of the general assembly only apply to agency ac(cid:415)ons
commenced under IC 4-21.5-3 a(cid:332)er June 30, 2023.”
10. In 2024, the Indiana legislature amended Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 for a second (cid:415)me. The
2024 amendments slightly modified the structure of Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 and changed
the “based on an invalid rule” language added in 2023 to “unsupported by a statute or valid
rule”. See Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5(a)(2) (2024). The 2024 amendment also included the
addi(cid:415)on of subsec(cid:415)on (b) which allows for a trial court to award reasonable a(cid:425)orney’s fees in
a judicial review proceeding. See Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5(b) (2024). The 2024 amendments
took effect on July 1, 2024.
11. In its Request for an Award of A(cid:425)orney’s Fees, NIM ini(cid:415)ally concedes that the 2023 and 2024
amendments to Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 do not apply to this proceeding pursuant to Ind.
Code § 4-21.5-2-8. See NIM’s Request for Award of A(cid:425)orney’s Fees, footnote 3. NIM then
argues that it is en(cid:415)tled to an award of a(cid:425)orney’s fees under Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5, as
originally enacted in 2021, because the agency ac(cid:415)on at issue here was frivolous and
groundless. Conversely, in its Reply to IDEM’s Response to NIM’s Request for A(cid:425)orney’s Fees,
NIM changes course and argues that it is asking the OALP to award a(cid:425)orney’s fees under
subparts (a)(1)(A) and (a)(3) of Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5, cites to the 2024 version of the
statute, and proffers that Judge Joven’s Order Gran(cid:415)ng Relief on Judicial Review confirms not
only that IDEM’s ac(cid:415)on was frivolous or groundless but that it is equally evident that the IDEM
has not demonstrated that it acted within its legal authority.
12. “Whether a statute or amendment is to be applied retroac(cid:415)vely to pending cases or only
prospec(cid:415)vely depends upon the legislature's intent. Absent an express indica(cid:415)on otherwise,
we presume that the legislature intends statutes and amendments to apply prospec(cid:415)vely.”
Chesnut v. Roof, 665 N.E.2d 7, 9 (Ind. Ct. App. 1996). See also Guzzo v. Town of St. John, 131
N.E.3d 179, 180 (Ind. 2019). As more fully explained by the Indiana Court Appeals in Indiana
Bureau of Motor Vehicles v. Watson, 70 N.E.3d 380, 385 (Ind. Ct. App. 2017):
The general rule in Indiana is that “[s]tatutes are to be given prospec(cid:415)ve effect
only, unless the legislature unequivocally and unambiguously intended
retrospec(cid:415)ve effect as well.” State v. Pelley, 828 N.E.2d 915, 919 (Ind. 2005). An
excep(cid:415)on to this general rule exists for remedial or procedural statutes. Mar(cid:415)n v.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-1912-000556
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 5 of 8
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689
2025 OALP 065, page 070

State, 774 N.E.2d 43, 44 (Ind. 2002). Although statutes and rules that are
procedural or remedial may be applied retroac(cid:415)vely, they are not required to be.
Pelley, 828 N.E.2d at 919. Even for procedural or remedial statutes, “retroac(cid:415)ve
applica(cid:415)on is the excep(cid:415)on, and such laws are normally to be applied
prospec(cid:415)vely absent strong and compelling reasons.” Hurst v. State, 890 N.E.2d
88, 95 (Ind. Ct. App. 2008) (quota(cid:415)on omi(cid:425)ed), trans. denied.
A remedial statute is a statute enacted to cure a defect, clear up any confusion and/or mischief
in the prior law, or address silence in a statute. See N.G. v. State, 148 N.E.3d 971, 973 (Ind.
2020), Lawrence v. State, 214 N.E.3d 361, 363 (Ind. 2023), Mar(cid:415)n v. State, 774 N.E.2d 43, 44
(Ind. 2002). A procedural statute is a statute that “prescribes the method of enforcing a right
or obtaining redress for invasion of that right” as opposed to a substan(cid:415)ve statute which
“creates, defines and regulates rights.” Morrison v. Vasquez, 124 N.E.3d 1217, 1222 (Ind.
2019) ci(cid:415)ng Hayden v. State, 771 N.E.2d 100, 102 (Ind. Ct. App. 2002).
13. The Indiana legislature did not specify that Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 should be given
retrospec(cid:415)ve effect when originally enacted in 2021. Nothing in the plain language of the
statute itself – as originally enacted or as it reads today - indicates an unequivocal and
unambiguous retrospec(cid:415)ve intent. In fact, the only unequivocal and unambiguous intent
expressed by the legislature as to Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 is that it is not to be given
retrospec(cid:415)ve effect. See Ind. Code § 4-21.5-2-8.
14. Further, Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 is neither procedural nor remedial. It was not enacted to
cure any defect, clear up confusion, or speak to silence in a preexis(cid:415)ng statute – it was a new
provision enacted to create a new right to a(cid:425)orney's fees outside of the American rule where
none existed previously. Nor does it prescribe a method of enforcing a right or obtaining
redress. Rather, Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 creates, defines, and regulates a party’s right to
a(cid:425)orney’s fees in an adjudica(cid:415)ve proceeding under AOPA and is thereby substan(cid:415)ve. Because
Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 is a substan(cid:415)ve statute, the exclusion to the general rule does not
apply.
15. NIM has not presented any evidence or argument to show that Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 – as
originally enacted or as amended - was intended to have retrospec(cid:415)ve effect. Similarly, NIM
has not presented any evidence or argument that Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 is procedural or
remedial thereby excep(cid:415)ng it from the general rule that statutes are to be given prospec(cid:415)ve
effect only and are not to be applied retroac(cid:415)vely.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-1912-000556
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 6 of 8
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689
2025 OALP 065, page 071

16. Accordingly, Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 may not be applied retroac(cid:415)vely to create an
en(cid:415)tlement to a(cid:425)orney’s fees in proceedings commenced prior to its enactment and is
thereby inapplicable to this proceeding.
17. NIM has failed to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that it is en(cid:415)tled to an award of
a(cid:425)orney’s fees under Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5.
Decision and Order
NIM is not en(cid:415)tled to a(cid:425)orney’s fees under Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27.5 and as such, it is
hereby ORDERED that NIM‘s Request for an Award of A(cid:425)orney’s Fees is DENIED.
SO ORDERED on: July 15, 2025.
Administra(cid:415)ve Law Judge
Hon. Vanessa Voigt Gould
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-1912-000556
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 7 of 8
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689
2025 OALP 065, page 072

Appeal Rights
A person who wishes to seek judicial review of this final determina(cid:415)on must file a pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for
review in an appropriate court within 30 days of the date this Order was served. See Ind. Code §
4-21.5-5-5. Guidance for calcula(cid:415)ng deadlines may be found at Indiana Code § 4-21.5-3-2.
Other requirements for a pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for judicial review may be found at Indiana Code chapter 4-
21.5-5. A pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for judicial review must be served on the Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law at
oalp@oalp.in.gov to ensure the Office prepares the record that will be filed in the court
presiding over the judicial review.

STATE OF INDIANA

FINAL ORDER ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT
The Administra(cid:415)ve Law Judge (“ALJ”) Vanessa Voigt Gould, having reviewed the record
and Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner Oakland Holdings, LLC’s (“Oakland”) Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment, brief in
support, designa(cid:415)on of evidence, and reply, as well as Respondents’ responses in opposi(cid:415)on and
counter designa(cid:415)ons, now issues this Final Order on Summary Judgment as it relates to the
Indiana Department of Environmental Management’s (“IDEM”) gran(cid:415)ng of Industrial Waste
Products Compos(cid:415)ng and Marke(cid:415)ng and Distribu(cid:415)on Permit No. IN LA 000909 (the “Permit”).
Any aggrieved party may appeal this decision. Appeal instruc(cid:415)ons are at the end of this
document.
Jurisdic(cid:415)on
The ALJ assigned to this proceeding by the Director of the Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law
Proceedings (“OALP”), see Ind. Code § 4-15-10.5-13, has jurisdic(cid:415)on over this case pursuant to
Indiana Code § 4-15-10.5-12, which gives OALP jurisdic(cid:415)on over agency administra(cid:415)ve ac(cid:415)ons
subject to the Indiana Administra(cid:415)ve Orders and Procedures Act at Indiana Code Art. 4-21.5
(“AOPA”) or “any other statute that requires or allows the office to take ac(cid:415)on.” The OALP has
jurisdic(cid:415)on over this case because this case is governed by AOPA.

Issues
The following issues were presented by the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner, Oakland Holdings, LLC (“Oakland”)
on Summary Judgment:
1. Whether the Permit unlawfully allows Organics to construct and operate a solid waste
processing facility without a solid waste processing permit in viola(cid:415)on of 329 IAC 11-9.
2. Whether the Permit unlawfully allows Organics to construct and operate a compost facility
without a compos(cid:415)ng facility registra(cid:415)on in viola(cid:415)on of Indiana Code § 13-20-10-2.
3. Whether the Permit violates Ind. Code § 13-20-10-9.
4. Whether the Permit violates 327 IAC 6.1-5-3.
5. Whether the Permit violates 327 IAC 6.1-5-2.
6. Whether IDEM’s applica(cid:415)on of the Land Applica(cid:415)on Rule and default standards in issuing the
Permit was arbitrary and/or unlawful.
7. Whether the Permit violates Indiana Code § 13-18-12-2.5.
8. Whether the Permit violates 327 IAC 6.1-8-6.
9. Whether the Permit violates Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1.
Procedural History
1. On November 30, 2023, IDEM issued Industrial Waste Products Compos(cid:415)ng and Marke(cid:415)ng
and Distribu(cid:415)on Permit No. IN LA 000909 (the Permit) to Organics Southern, LLC (“Organics”).1
2. On December 8, 2023, Oakland, an adjacent property owner, filed a Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for
Administra(cid:415)ve Review and Stay with the Office of Environmental Adjudica(cid:415)on.
3. On February 15, 2024, Oakland filed an Amended Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for Administra(cid:415)ve Review and Stay.
4. On January 31, 2025, Oakland filed its Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment, Brief in Support, and
Designa(cid:415)on of Evidence.
1 IDEM Ex. 1, Organics Ex. 8.

5. On March 3, 2025, Organics filed a Brief Opposing Oakland’s Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment
and Designa(cid:415)on of Counter Evidence.
6. Also on March 3, 2025, IDEM filed its Response to Oakland’s Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment
and a Designa(cid:415)on of Evidence.
7. On March 17, 2025, Oakland filed its Reply in Support of Summary Judgment.
8. On March 7, 2025, Oakland filed a Mo(cid:415)on for Extension of Time to file a Reply in Support of
Summary Judgment that was subsequently granted.
9. Oral Arguments were heard on the Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment on March 26, 2025.
10. On May 29, 2025, ALJ Lori Kyle Endris issued an Order requiring the par(cid:415)es file Proposed
Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law by June 12, 2025.
11. This ma(cid:425)er was then reassigned from ALJ Lori Kyle Endris to ALJ Vanessa Voigt Gould.
12. On June 12, 2025, the par(cid:415)es filed their respec(cid:415)ve Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions
of Law and the record on Summary Judgment closed.
Findings of Fact
1. The Findings of Fact stated herein are undisputed.
2. On February 22, 2023, Organics submi(cid:425)ed a marke(cid:415)ng and distribu(cid:415)on permit applica(cid:415)on to
IDEM (“Applica(cid:415)on”) under 327 IAC 6.1-5.2
3. Through the Applica(cid:415)on, Organics sought IDEM approval to construct a compost facility at
3155 Wesley Road, Boonville, Warrick County, Indiana (“Site”), receive and process and/or
compost industrial waste product and other materials, and market and distribute the finished
compost as a landscaping or soil amendment.3
4. The Site is adjacent to real property owned by Oakland that has been approved for a primary
plat for a residen(cid:415)al subdivision containing 57 lots. Oakland maintains its property will be
adversely impacted by Organics’ construc(cid:415)on and opera(cid:415)on of the Site under the Permit.4
2 Oakland Ex. C, pp. 19:17-22, 121-137.
3 Oakland Ex. C, pp. 83:7-9, 130, 139-141; Oakland Ex. E, p. 83:11-14; Oakland Ex. A, Organics’ Resp. to RFAs 14 and
22; IDEM Ex. 2, Organics, Ex. 4.
4 Oakland Ex. F, pp. 28-30, 49-51, 111-12, 114-15.

5. At the (cid:415)me Organics submi(cid:425)ed its Applica(cid:415)on to IDEM, the Applica(cid:415)on was incomplete in
that it was missing informa(cid:415)on required under 327 IAC 6.1-5-3.5
6. Specifically, the Applica(cid:415)on did not contain the following informa(cid:415)on relevant to how
industrial waste products would be stored at the Site: (1) slope; (2) the water table; (3) soil
pH. The Applica(cid:415)on also did not contain any analy(cid:415)cal tes(cid:415)ng results or laboratory analysis
for the industrial waste products that would be received at the Site for processing and/or
compos(cid:415)ng.6
7. During the permi(cid:427)ng process, IDEM requested some addi(cid:415)onal informa(cid:415)on and/or
documenta(cid:415)on from Organics.7 In response to IDEM’s requests, Organics supplemented its
Applica(cid:415)on on mul(cid:415)ple occasions.8
8. In March 2023, Organics supplemented its Applica(cid:415)on by providing addi(cid:415)onal informa(cid:415)on on
the no(cid:415)ce given to adjoining property owners, the physical loca(cid:415)on address for the Site that
had previously been omi(cid:425)ed, and new language on the receipt of addi(cid:415)onal industrial waste.9
9. In June of 2023, Organics supplemented its Applica(cid:415)on by providing a Master Opera(cid:415)ons Plan
to IDEM.10
10. Then, in Sepetmber and October of 2023, Organics further supplemented its applica(cid:415)on by

calcula(cid:415)ons.11

waste products will be stored at the Site to IDEM.12
12. IDEM was able to verify the topography – including slope informa(cid:415)on - for the Site using GIS
and/or other available online resources during the permi(cid:427)ng process.13

13. The purpose of slope informa(cid:415)on being required in the management plan is to consider

14. During the permi(cid:427)ng process, Organics did not provide IDEM with informa(cid:415)on on the water

15. The purpose of the water table informa(cid:415)on being required in a management plan is to

18. IDEM generally requires slopes, water table informa(cid:415)on, and soil borings to be submi(cid:425)ed with
the applica(cid:415)on during the permi(cid:427)ng process and before a Permit is approved and/or issued.19

dewatered; (2) meet the heavy metal limits detailed in Table 3 in 327 IAC 6.1-4-9(c); or (3)
meet the Polychlorinated Biphenyl (“PCB”) limit of 2 milligrams per kilogram on a dry weight
basis.21

mandatory rather than directory unless it is “clear from the context clear from the context or
the purpose of the statute that the legislature intended a different meaning.” United Rural
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2312-003076
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 31 of 35
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

Elec. Membership Corp. v. Indiana & Michigan Elec. Co., 549 N.E.2d 1019, 1022 (Ind. 1990)
ci(cid:415)ng State ex rel. City of Indianapolis v. Brennan, 109 N.E.2d 409 (1952); see also Hancock
County Rural Elec. v. City of Greenfield, 494 N.E.2d 1294, 1295 (Ind.Ct.App.1986), trans.
denied. This is why the word “shall” has o(cid:332)en been held to be directory rather than
mandatory. See May v. DNR, 565 N.E.2d 367, 371 (Ind. Ct. App 1991).
94. The meaning and inten(cid:415)on of the legislature may be ascertained from the language of the
statute itself but also by considering its “its design, its nature and the consequences that flow
from the various interpreta(cid:415)ons.” State v. Langen, 708 N.E.2d 617, 621–22 (Ind. Ct. App. 1999)
ci(cid:415)ng Allen County Dept. of Pub. Welfare v. Ball Memorial Hosp. Ass'n, 253 Ind. 179, 184
(1969).
“All laws are mandatory in the sense that a duty of obedience is imposed, but it
does not follow that every slight departure is fatal where the act is merely
procedural and does not go to the merits. The basic test, we believe, to determine
whether the requirement is essen(cid:415)al or not, is to consider the consequences of
the failure to follow the statute and, in this regard, other possible interpreta(cid:415)ons.”
Id. Accordingly, “when a statute contains no nega(cid:415)ve or prohibi(cid:415)ve words and does not
provide for penal(cid:415)es on the consequences for the failure to follow prescribed (cid:415)me limits,
those limits may be merely directory.” Id.
95. IDEM issued the Permit 271 days a(cid:332)er Organics filed its ini(cid:415)al applica(cid:415)on and a(cid:332)er the
expira(cid:415)on of the 180-day (cid:415)me frame allo(cid:425)ed under Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1. However,
Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1 contains no nega(cid:415)ve or prohibi(cid:415)ve words and similarly does not
provide for nega(cid:415)ve consequences or penal(cid:415)es - other than those listed in Indiana Code § 13-
15-4-11(b) - for a failure by IDEM to approve or deny a marke(cid:415)ng and distribu(cid:415)on permit
within 180 days. Indiana Code § 13-15-4-11(b) makes it clear that the 180-day (cid:415)me period
stated in Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1 is directory not mandatory. Indiana Code § 13-15-4-11(b)
also makes it clear that IDEM retains the authority to approve or deny a marke(cid:415)ng and
distribu(cid:415)on permit a(cid:332)er 180 days.
96. Further, in interpre(cid:415)ng “statutory language, we must presume that the legislature did not
intend an unreasonable and absurd result.” Langen, 708 N.E.2d 617 ci(cid:415)ng Chesnut v.
Roof, 665 N.E.2d 7, 10 (Ind.Ct.App.1996). To construe the “shall” in Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1
as mandatory would ignore the legislature’s clear inten(cid:415)on that IDEM retains authority to
approve or a deny a marke(cid:415)ng and distribu(cid:415)on permit a(cid:332)er 180 days. Ind. Code § 13-15-4-
11(b). Such a result would be unreasonable and absurd.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2312-003076
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 32 of 35
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

97. Because the 180-day statutorily prescribed (cid:415)me period imposed by Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1
is directory, and because IDEM retains authority to approve or deny a marke(cid:415)ng and
distribu(cid:415)on permit beyond the 180 days, IDEM was not required to deny the Applica(cid:415)on.
98. Oakland has failed to show by substan(cid:415)al evidence that IDEM’s statutory power to issue the
Permit expired with the 180-day deadline and/or that the Permit violates Ind. Code § 13-15-
4-1 as a ma(cid:425)er of law. Accordingly, Oakland’s request for summary judgment in this issue is
DENIED.
99. Further, the undisputed facts demonstrate that IDEM and Organics are en(cid:415)tled to judgment
as a ma(cid:425)er of law. As such, summary judgment on this issue is GRANTED in favor of IDEM and
Organics.
Decision and Order
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED THAT Oakland’s Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment is granted in part
and denied in part.
Summary Judgment is entered in favor of IDEM and Organics on the following issues:
1. Whether the Permit unlawfully allows Organics to construct and operate a solid waste
processing facility without a solid waste processing permit in viola(cid:415)on of 329 IAC 11-9.
2. Whether the Permit unlawfully allows Organics to construct and operate a compost facility
without a compos(cid:415)ng facility registra(cid:415)on in viola(cid:415)on of Indiana Code § 13-20-10-2.
3. Whether the Permit violates Ind. Code § 13-20-10-9.
4. Whether the Permit violates 327 IAC 6.1-5-2.
5. Whether IDEM’s applica(cid:415)on of the Land Applica(cid:415)on Rule and certain default standards in
issuing the Permit was arbitrary and/or unlawful.
6. Whether the Permit violates Indiana Code § 13-18-12-2.5.
7. Whether the Permit violates 327 IAC 6.1-8-6.
8. Whether the Permit violates Indiana Code § 13-15-4-1.
However, summary judgment is hereby entered in favor of Oakland on the issue of
whether the Permit violates 327 IAC 6.1-5-3. In approving the Applica(cid:415)on and issuing the Permit
absent the loca(cid:415)on criteria informa(cid:415)on required under 327 IAC 6.1-5-3, IDEM failed to follow the
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2312-003076
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 33 of 35
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

applicable rules and regula(cid:415)ons for issuing a marke(cid:415)ng and distribu(cid:415)on permit. Consequently,
IDEM’s approval of the Applica(cid:415)on and issuance of the Permit was invalid. The Permit is therefore
overturned. Nothing in this opinion shall be construed to prevent Organics from obtaining a valid
Permit for the Site in the future.
SO ORDERED on: September 10, 2025.

ISSUED:
STATE OF INDIANA

FINAL ORDER GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT
The Administra(cid:415)ve Law Judge (“ALJ”) Vanessa Voigt Gould, having reviewed the record
and the pleadings filed by the par(cid:415)es on Summary Judgment, now issues this Final Order as it
relates to the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for Administra(cid:415)ve Review filed by David Cole (“Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner”) on the 327 IAC
3 Construc(cid:415)on Permit, Page Road Sanitary Extension, Permit Approval No. 25694, issued to the
Town of Grabill (“Town”) by the Indiana Department of Environmental Management (“IDEM”) on
February 10, 2025. This decision is favorable to the Town and the IDEM (referred to collec(cid:415)vely
below as “Respondents”). Any aggrieved party may appeal this decision. Appeal instruc(cid:415)ons are
at the end of this document.
Jurisdic(cid:415)on
The ALJ assigned to this proceeding by the Director of the Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law
Proceedings (“OALP”), see Ind. Code § 4-15-10.5-13, has jurisdic(cid:415)on over this case pursuant to
Indiana Code § 4-15-10.5-12, which gives the OALP jurisdic(cid:415)on over agency administra(cid:415)ve ac(cid:415)ons
subject to the Indiana Administra(cid:415)ve Orders and Procedures Act at Indiana Code Art. 4-21.5
(“AOPA”) or “any other statute that requires or allows the office to take ac(cid:415)on.” The OALP has
jurisdic(cid:415)on over this case because this case is governed by AOPA.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No.: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204

Issue
Whether, based on the undisputed material facts in the recod, the Respondents are
en(cid:415)tled to judgment as a ma(cid:425)er of law on the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for Review filed by the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner seeking
administra(cid:415)ve review of the 327 IAC 3 Construc(cid:415)on Permit, Page Road Sanitary Extension, Permit
Approval No. 25694 (the “Permit”), issued to the Town by the IDEM on February 10, 2025.
Procedural History
1. On February 10, 2025, IDEM issued an Authoriza(cid:415)on for Construc(cid:415)on of Sanitary Sewer
System Under 327 IAC 3, Permit Approval No. 25694 (the “Permit”).
2. A pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for administra(cid:415)ve review of the Permit was filed by Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner with the OALP on
February 28, 2025.
3. The OALP assigned ALJ Lori Kyle Endris to preside over this ma(cid:425)er that same day.
4. ALJ Endris issued a No(cid:415)ce of Insufficient Filing (“NOI”) on March 3, 2025.
5. On March 6, 2025, this ma(cid:425)er was reassigned to ALJ Vanessa Voigt Gould and an Order
was issued affirming the NOI.
6. On April 7, 2025, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner supplemented and/or amended his Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for Review.
7. An Ini(cid:415)al Prehearing Conference was held in this ma(cid:425)er on April 24, 2025.
8. On August 25, 2025, the Respondents filed a Joint Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment and
Memorandum of Law in Support of their Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment which included
the designa(cid:415)on of one exhibit, Respondents’ Exhibit A, the Permit Applica(cid:415)on Package for
Permit Approval 25694, VCF #83763768 (56 pages).
9. On September 24, 2025, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner filed a Response to Summary Judgment and counter
designa(cid:415)on of evidence. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s counter designa(cid:415)on of evidence was nearly iden(cid:415)cal
to Respondents’ Exhibit A referenced above, however, it varied in that Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner had
added comments and/or notes to the document.
10. On October 9, 2025, the Respondents filed a Reply in Support of their Mo(cid:415)on for Summary
Judgment and the record on summary judgment closed.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The following are undisputed material facts:
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 2 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

1. On November 5, 2024, the Town submi(cid:425)ed an applica(cid:415)on for a construc(cid:415)on permit to the
IDEM proposing to build a low-pressure sanitary sewer system (Respondents’ Exhibit A to
Respondents’ Brief in Support of Mo(cid:415)on for Summary Judgment (“Respondents’ Exhibit
A”), pp. 10-22).
2. The applica(cid:415)on sought to extend an exis(cid:415)ng sanitary sewer system along Page Road in the
Town of Grabill, Indiana (Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 2).
3. The Town supplemented its applica(cid:415)on on December 2, 2024, through the submission of
plans and specifica(cid:415)ons that were prepared by DLZ Indiana, LLC and cer(cid:415)fied by Casey
Erwin, Professional Engineer (Respondents’ Exhibit A, pp. 2, 23-25).
4. The Town later supplied addi(cid:415)onal informa(cid:415)on to the IDEM and submi(cid:425)ed a revised
applica(cid:415)on on February 3, 2025 (Respondents’ Exhibit A, pp. 2, 26-56).
5. On February 10, 2025, IDEM issued an Authoriza(cid:415)on for Construc(cid:415)on of Sanitary Sewer
System Under 327 IAC 3, Permit Approval No. 25694 (the “Permit”) (Respondents’ Exhibit
A, pp. 2-9).
6. The Permit authorizes the construc(cid:415)on of a low-pressure sanitary sewer system along
Page Road extending approximately 3,665 feet south from the intersec(cid:415)on with Witmer
Road and along Witmer Road extending approximately 431 feet east from the intersec(cid:415)on
with Page Road (the “Project”) (Respondents’ Exhibit A, pp. 2 and 5).
7. The Project involves the installa(cid:415)on of approximately 56 feet of 10-inch diameter PVC
(ASTM D3034 SDR-35) sanitary sewer and approximately 4,105 feet of 3-inch small
diameter HDPE (ASTM D3035 DR9, 250 PSI) low-pressure sewer (Respondents’ Exhibit A,
p. 5).
8. Under the Permit, the Project may provide sewer service for 31 single family homes
(Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 5).
9. The Permit requires privately owned simplex grinder pump sta(cid:415)ons to be installed on each
residen(cid:415)al property that will be serviced by the Project (Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 5).
10. The Permit requires that the owners of each residen(cid:415)al property serviced by the Project
will be responsible for installing, providing power to, and maintaining the grinder pump
sta(cid:415)ons as well as the lateral service lines up to the connec(cid:415)on with the public sewer main
at the right-of-way line (Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 5).
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 3 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

11. The Permit encompasses only the public por(cid:415)on of the low-pressure sanitary sewer
system (Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 5).
12. Under the Permit, the Town is responsible for inspec(cid:415)ng the sewer installa(cid:415)on and for the
maintenance of public por(cid:415)on of the low-pressure sanitary sewer system a(cid:332)er the Project
is completed (Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 5).
13. In addi(cid:415)on to imposing specific and general terms and condi(cid:415)ons, the Permit requires the
Project to conform to all provisions of 327 IAC 3 (Respondents’ Exhibit A, pp. 2-9).
14. The Permit may be modified, suspended, or revoked for cause including, but not limited
to, viola(cid:415)ons of any of the terms and/or condi(cid:415)ons and for misrepresenta(cid:415)on or failure
to fully disclose all relevant facts during the permi(cid:427)ng process (Respondents’ Exhibit A,
p. 6).
15. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner owns certain real property located on Page Road that may be affected by the
Permit and/or Project (Respondents’ Exhibit A, p. 17).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. This is a Final Order issued under Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-23. Findings of fact that may be
construed as conclusions of law and conclusions of law that may be construed as findings
of fact are so deemed.
2. The OALP has jurisdic(cid:415)on over and serves as the ul(cid:415)mate authority for administra(cid:415)ve
reviews of permits issued by the IDEM. See Indiana Code § 4-21.5, Ind. Code § 4-15-10.5-
12. In addi(cid:415)on, administra(cid:415)ve reviews of permits issued by the IDEM are governed by 315
IAC 1, et. seq.
3. Pursuant to Ind. Code § 4–21.5–3–14(c) “[a]t each stage of the proceeding, the agency or
other person requesting that an agency take action or asserting an affirmative defense
specified by law has the burden of persuasion and the burden of going forward with the
proof of the request or affirmative defense.” The party who has the burden of proof will
be required to prove their case by a preponderance of the evidence. Ind. Code § 4-21.5-
5-14, see also Huffman v. Office of Envtl. Adjud., 811 N.E.2d 806, 809 (Ind. 2004).
4. The ALJ must apply a de novo standard of review when determining the facts at issue.
Indiana Dept. of Natural Resources v. United Refuse Co., Inc., 615 N.E.2d 100 (Ind. 1993).
Findings of fact must be based exclusively on the evidence presented on the record and/or
ma(cid:425)ers that are officially no(cid:415)ced by the presiding ALJ - deference to the agency’s ini(cid:415)al
factual determina(cid:415)on is not allowed. Id.; Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-27(d). Further, OALP is
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 4 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

required to base its findings of fact on substan(cid:415)al and reliable evidence. Ind. Code § 4-
21.5-3-27(d).
5. At any (cid:415)me a(cid:332)er the ALJ is assigned to the case, a party may move for summary judgment
in that party’s favor. Ind. Code § 4-21.5-23.
6. Pursuant to Ind. Code § 4-21.5-3-23, an ALJ shall consider a summary judgment mo(cid:415)on
as would a court that is considering a mo(cid:415)on for summary judgment filed under Rule 56
of the Indiana Rules of Trial Procedure.
7. The ALJ may grant summary judgment if it finds that “the designated eviden(cid:415)ary ma(cid:425)er
shows that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is
en(cid:415)tled to a judgment as a ma(cid:425)er of law.” Ind. Tr. R. 56(C); IC § 4-21.5-3-23.
8. “A fact is ‘material’ if its resolu(cid:415)on would affect the outcome of the case, and an issue is
‘genuine’ if a trier of fact is required to resolve the par(cid:415)es’ differing accounts of the truth
. . . or if the undisputed material facts support conflic(cid:415)ng reasonable inferences.” Williams
v. Tharp, 914 N.E.2d 756, 761 (Ind. 2009) (internal cita(cid:415)ons omi(cid:425)ed).
9. The moving party bears the burden of establishing that summary judgment is appropriate.
All facts and inferences must be construed in favor of the non-movant, and all doubts as
to the existence of a material issue must be resolved against the moving party. Gibson v.
Evansville Vanderburgh Building Commission, et al., 725 N.E.2d 949 (Ind. Ct. App. 2000);
City of North Vernon v. Jennings Northwest Regional U(cid:415)li(cid:415)es, 829 N.E.2d 1, (Ind. 2005);
Tibbs v. Huber, Hunt & Nichols, Inc., 668 N.E.2d 248, 249 (Ind. 1996).
10. A party opposing summary judgment must present specific facts demonstra(cid:415)ng a genuine
issue for trial. Hale v. Community Hospitals of Indianapolis, 567 N.E.2d 842, 843 (Ind. Ct.
App. 1991). When a mo(cid:415)on for summary judgment is made, an adverse party may not
rest upon the mere allega(cid:415)ons or denials of their pleading but must set forth specific facts
showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. Williams, 914 N.E.2d 756 (Ind. 2009).
11. Mere asser(cid:415)ons, opinions, or conclusions of law will not suffice to create a genuine issue
of material fact to preclude summary judgment. Sanchez v. Hamara, 534 N.E.2d 756, 758
(Ind. Ct. App. 1989), trans. denied; McMahan v. Snap-On Tool Corp., 478 N.E.2d 116, 122
(Ind. Ct. App. 1985).
12. The IDEM is a state agency that implements and enforces specified Indiana environmental
laws, and rules promulgated relevant to those laws, per Indiana Code § 13-13-1-1, et seq.
and Indiana Code § 13-14-1-1, et seq. These statutes also give the IDEM authority to
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 5 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

review and issue certain permits. See Ind. Code § 13-15-1, et. seq. The IDEM is authorized
to determine whether a permit should be issued by applying the relevant statutes and
regula(cid:415)ons pertaining to permits and can only consider said statutes and regula(cid:415)ons
when deciding whether to issue the permit. See American Suburban U(cid:415)li(cid:415)es, 2019 OEA
48, 53.
13. The Town is a municipality with powers, granted by the General Assembly, that are
necessary or desirable in the conduct of its affairs. See Ind. Code § 36-1-2-11; Ind. Code §
36-1-3-4. Specifically, the Town has explicit power to “acquire, construct, improve,
operate, and maintain sewage works.” See Ind. Code § 36-9-23-2. In an exercise of this
power, the Town submi(cid:425)ed an applica(cid:415)on to IDEM for a permit to construct a sanitary
sewer system along Page Road and Witmer Road.
14. Permits for the construc(cid:415)on of a sanitary sewer are required by and governed by the
requirements that are laid out 327 IAC 3. Administra(cid:415)ve review of a permit issued by the
IDEM is limited to whether IDEM acted in conformity with controlling statutes and
regula(cid:415)ons. See Aqua Indiana, Inc., 2010 OEA 168, ci(cid:415)ng In re: Objec(cid:415)on to Issuance of
Sec(cid:415)on 401 Water Quality Cer(cid:415)fica(cid:415)on COE ID No. 198800247 Conagra Soybean
Processing Co., 1998 WL 918585, at *3, OEA Cause No. 98-W-J-2052 (Nov. 12, 1988).
15. 315 IAC 1-3-2(b)(4)(A) requires a pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner in a case involving an administra(cid:415)ve appeal of
the issuance a permit to state with par(cid:415)cularity and iden(cid:415)fy:
(i) Environmental concerns or technical deficiencies related to the ac(cid:415)on of
the commissioner that is the subject of the pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on.
(ii) Permit terms and condi(cid:415)ons that the pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner contends would be
appropriate to comply with the law applicable to the contested permit.
16. Whenever a permit is required by any rule of the environmental rules board under Indiana
Code § 13-15-1 for the construc(cid:415)on, installa(cid:415)on, opera(cid:415)on, or modifica(cid:415)on of any facility,
equipment, or device, the permit may be issued only a(cid:332)er the IDEM has: (1) approved the
plans and specifica(cid:415)ons; and (2) determined that the facility, equipment, or device meets
the requirements of the applicable rule. Ind. Code § 13-15-3-5.
17. The undisputed facts in this ma(cid:425)er demonstrate that the IDEM reviewed and approved
the plans and specifica(cid:415)ons for the Project. The Town submi(cid:425)ed plans and specifica(cid:415)ons
to the IDEM during the permi(cid:427)ng process. Those plans and specifica(cid:415)ons - including the
design summary - were reviewed and approved by the IDEM through its issuance of the
Permit. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has failed to present any argument or evidence to the contrary.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 6 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

18. The undisputed facts also demonstrate that Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has failed to allege, with the
required specificity, any way in which the Permit does not meet the requirements of the
applicable rule - 327 IAC 3. Specifically, neither the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on nor the
supplement/amendment thereto cite to any provision of 327 IAC 3 or to any specific
Permit term or condi(cid:415)on that the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner deems deficient under the law as required by
315 IAC 1-3-2. Further, neither the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on nor the supplement/amendment thereto
state, with par(cid:415)cularity, any environmental concern or technical defect related to IDEM’s
issuance of the Permit that stands in contraven(cid:415)on of 327 IAC 3 as required by 315 IAC 1-
3-2. Instead, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has alleged that the Town has not set forth evidence as to how
people without u(cid:415)lity service – par(cid:415)cularly the Amish property owners on Page Road -
will be able to install the required electric grinder pump sta(cid:415)ons, argued affected property
owners were not given informa(cid:415)on, and expressed various concerns related to the design
and future func(cid:415)onality of the Project should there be addi(cid:415)onal expansion.
19. It is important to note that under the applicable Indiana law, a pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on for review of an
IDEM ac(cid:415)on must state with par(cid:415)cularity the issues proposed for considera(cid:415)on. See 315
IAC 1-3-2(a)(4); Ind. Code § 13-15-6-2(5). Issues not properly raised in the pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on are
waived. Bd. of Comm'rs of LaPorte Cnty. v. Great Lakes Transfer, LLC, 888 N.E.2d 784, 795
(Ind. Ct. App. 2008). As such, the issues raised by Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner in the summary judgment
proceedings that were not raised by the Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)on or the supplement/amendment thereto,
have been waived. However, even if the arguments had not been waived, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s
arguments fail nonetheless.
20. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s argument that the Town has not set forth evidence as to how people without
u(cid:415)lity service – par(cid:415)cularly the Amish property owners on Page Road - will be able to
install the required electric grinder pump sta(cid:415)ons is outside the scope of 327 IAC 3 and
fails to state a claim upon which relief may be granted. 327 IAC 3 does not require a
permi(cid:425)ee to show that future users of a sanitary sewer system have u(cid:415)lity power and/or
possess sufficient power to operate grinder pump sta(cid:415)ons (if required) for a construc(cid:415)on
permit to be issued. As such, the Town was not required to provide such evidence or
informa(cid:415)on nor was the IDEM authorized to require it as a condi(cid:415)on precedent to
approving the Town’s applica(cid:415)on and issuing the Permit. The only applicable requirement
contained within 327 IAC 3 related to grinder pumps states that an applicant must indicate
who will be responsible for maintaining the grinder pumps. See 327 IAC 3-2-2(e)(5); see
also Page Road, 2022 OEA 150, 154. The Town did precisely that when it noted in its
applica(cid:415)on that the grinder pumps would be privately owned and maintained.
21. Further, it is undisputed that the Permit at issue mandates compliance with its terms and
condi(cid:415)ons as well as 327 IAC 3. Under the Permit’s terms and condi(cid:415)ons, grinder pump
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 7 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

sta(cid:415)ons are required for each lateral line and/or property that seeks to connect to the
main sewer line. If a property owner does not have enough power to run a grinder pump
sta(cid:415)on as detailed in the Permit, that property cannot connect to the main line nor can it
send wastewater into the proposed sewer system. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s specula(cid:415)on that future
users may not have enough power to run the required pump sta(cid:415)ons is not a sufficient
basis for challenging or overturning the Permit. See Jennings, 909 N.E.2d at 1026. See also
DeGroot Dairy, 2006 OEA 1; Ge(cid:425)elfinger, 2005 OEA 1; Lafolle(cid:425)e Sta(cid:415)on Towne Centre,
2004 OEA 67; Grahn, 2004 OEA 40.
22. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s argument that poten(cid:415)ally affected property owners were not given certain
informa(cid:415)on fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. For a sewer permit, an
applicant must submit one prepared mailing label for each poten(cid:415)ally affected person for
IDEM to mail no(cid:415)ce of the permit when issued. See 327 IAC 3-2-2(e)(6). Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has
offered no evidence that IDEM did not comply with this requirement in issuing the Permit.
23. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner also takes issue with certain perceived discrepancies between the Town’s ini(cid:415)al
applica(cid:415)on submi(cid:425)ed on November 5, 2024, and the revised applica(cid:415)on submi(cid:425)ed on
February 3, 2025. The undisputed facts show that a(cid:332)er the submission of its ini(cid:415)al
applica(cid:415)on, the Town submi(cid:425)ed addi(cid:415)onal informa(cid:415)on and documenta(cid:415)on to IDEM and
that on February 3, 2025, it submi(cid:425)ed a revised applica(cid:415)on. Allega(cid:415)ons that fail to raise
any issue concerning compliance with controlling legal requirements fail to state a valid
claim or sufficient basis for challenging or overturning the Permit. Aqua Indiana, Inc.,
supra, ci(cid:415)ng In re: Objec(cid:415)ons to Issuance of Public Water Supply Construc(cid:415)on Permit No.
WS-2924.
24. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s concerns related to the design of the Project fail for the same reason. See Id.
First, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has failed to present any evidence or argument that the design of the
Project does not comply with 327 IAC 3. While Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner a(cid:425)empts to argue that IDEM’s
approval of 3-inch pipe in lieu of 4-inch pipe for the Project was somehow improper, his
argument finds no support in the undisputed facts or law. Specifically, 327 IAC 3-6-32 gives
the IDEM authority to approve alterna(cid:415)ve technical standards and the undisputed facts
demonstrate that is exactly what was done here. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has offered no evidence that
the IDEM should not have approved the 3-inch pipe or that the 3-inch pipe violates any of
the provisions under 327 IAC 3. Further, Indiana law does not authorize the IDEM to
dictate the design of a sanitary sewer beyond the requirements promulgated in 327 IAC
3. See Page Road, 2022 OEA 150.
25. Similarly, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s concerns related to the future func(cid:415)onality of the Project should
there be an addi(cid:415)onal expansion also fails to state a valid claim or sufficient basis for
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 8 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

challenging or overturning the Permit. The first of Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s concerns related to
func(cid:415)onality centers on his unsupported belief that the Project will not be able to
accommodate the an(cid:415)cipated flow from the 31 equivalent dwelling units (“EDU”) noted
in the Permit. The undisputed facts show that the Project will poten(cid:415)ally receive flow from
78 Equivalent Dwelling Units (EDUs). Id. pp. 46-47. The Town’s calcula(cid:415)ons show that the
3-inch pipe for this ini(cid:415)al sewer line project will not only be capable of handling flow from
the 31 EDUs stated in the updated applica(cid:415)on and Permit but from future, increased flows
as well. Id. pp. 4, 10, 46-47. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has offered no evidence that the design flow
calcula(cid:415)ons are incorrect, that the approved system is insufficiently sized, or that IDEM’s
approval violates any provision under 327 IAC 3.
26. Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s second concern related to the future func(cid:415)onality of the Project is predicated
on his unsupported belief that that the Town has authority under Ind. Code § 36-9-23-30
to force, and will force, certain users to connect to the Project and will therefore
necessitate an addi(cid:415)onal expansion of the Project in upwards of ten to twenty years from
now. But whether the Town may have the authority under Ind. Code § 36-9-23-30.1 to
force connec(cid:415)ons to the Project has no relevance to IDEM’s issuance of the Permit. IDEM
approved the Permit under 327 IAC 3 based on the proposed design submi(cid:425)ed by the
Town for the Project. Should an expansion be required in the future, a new permit will
need to be obtained and meet the requirements of 327 IAC 3. Again, allega(cid:415)ons that fail
to raise any issue concerning compliance with controlling legal requirements fail to state
a valid claim. Aqua Indiana, Inc., supra, ci(cid:415)ng In re: Objec(cid:415)ons to Issuance of Public Water
Supply Construc(cid:415)on Permit No. WS-2924.
27. Finally, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner’s allega(cid:415)ons that the Town has not set forth evidence as to how people
without u(cid:415)lity service will be able to install the required electric grinder pump sta(cid:415)ons,
that affected property owners were not given informa(cid:415)on, and his concerns related to the
design and future func(cid:415)onality of the Project should there be addi(cid:415)onal expansion are
unsupported by the evidence, specula(cid:415)ve, and fail to create a ques(cid:415)on of fact that would
preclude summary judgment. See Bea(cid:425)y v. LaFountaine, 896 N.E.2d 18, 20 (Ind. Ct. App.
2008), Sanchez, 534 N.E.2d at 758, McMahan, 478 N.E.2d at 122.
28. For all of the foregoing reasons, Pe(cid:415)(cid:415)oner has failed to establish that the IDEM did not
comply with the applicable statutes and regula(cid:415)ons when issuing the Permit to the Town,
has failed to establish that the Permit does not comply with the requirements of 327 IAC
3, and has failed to state a viable claim for relief.
29. The designated evidence shows that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and
that the Respondents are en(cid:415)tled to a judgment as a ma(cid:425)er of law.
Office of Administra(cid:415)ve Law Proceedings Administra(cid:415)ve Case No: IDEM-2502-000857
100 N. Senate Ave., N-802, Indianapolis, IN 46204 9 of 11
oalp@oalp.in.gov | 317-234-6689

DECISION AND ORDER
For all of the foregoing reasons, IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED
that summary judgment in favor of the Respondents is appropriate. Respondents’ Mo(cid:415)on for
Summary Judgment is hereby GRANTED and summary judgment is entered in favor of the Town
and the IDEM. The Page Road Sanitary Extension, Permit Approval No. 25694 is therefore
AFFIRMED and all further proceedings in this ma(cid:425)er are VACATED.
SO ORDERED on: December 30, 2025.

NORTHERN INDIANA MANUFACTURING, INC.

CHESTERTON, PORTER COUNTY, INDIANA. )
FINDINGS OF FACT, CONCLUSIONS OF LAW and FINAL ORDER
This matter came before the Office of Environmental Adjudication (OEA or Court), by legal
counsels, Julie Lang, Esq. on the Indiana Department of Environmental Management’s (IDEM)
June 19, 2023 Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings1 and E. Sean Griggs, Esq., on Northern
Indiana Manufacturing, Inc.’s (Northern) Motion for Summary Judgment both of which
documents, along with their responses and replies are now part of the Court’s record. Oral
argument was held September 11, 2023. The presiding Environmental Law Judge (ELJ) having
read the Motions, Responses, Replies and supporting Briefs and directed the Oral Argument
now enters the following Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Final Order.
Findings of Fact
1. The property at issue is located at 914 Broadway Street, Chesterton, Porter County,
Indiana (Site) and has been used for industrial manufacturing from 1974 to the present.2
2. The previous owner Electro Seal Corporation,3 now Dynamic Alliance, Inc., (Dynamic)
1 Due to an Affidavit being presented to and accepted by the Court, IDEM’s Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
is considered a Motion for Summary Judgment. Ind. Trial Rule 12(C).
2 Petition for Administrative Review, Adjudicatory Hearing and Stay of Effectiveness (Petition), p. 2.
3 On November 29, 2023, the ELJ requested information from the counsels of record concerning the corporate
history of Electro Seal, Dynamic Alliance and Northern Indiana Manufacturing’s to clarify content of some of the
exhibits proffered in this Cause.
Northern’s counsel responded December 8, 2023 and disputed the Secretary of State’s records 197405-492 and
1990070580 stating that the records “appear to be a contradiction since the SOS would not have allowed two
identically named corporations to exist simultaneously.”
1
2024 OEA 001, page 002

owned and operated at the Site from approximately 1974 to 1996.4 The current owner,
Northern, leased the property in March, 1991 and purchased it in July, 1996.5
3. When Northern commenced operations at the Site, it became aware of potential
contamination and prompted Dynamic to undertake a Phase I Environmental Assessment.6
Thereafter, Northern hired Mittelhauser Corporation (Mittelhauser) to conduct a Phase II
Environmental Assessment which identified impacts to soil and groundwater.7 Mittelhauser’s
May 9, 1991, report stated in part, “The levels of tetrachloroethene (PCE) in groundwater
samples GW-2 and GW-3 are particularly significant.”8
4. On May 21, 1991, Northern wrote its attorney regarding the spill of PCE, stating “[t]his is
all related to 1978. Longer ago than I expected.”9
5. On June 4, 1991, Northern sent Dynamic a letter “asserting a claim for indemnification
by Dynamic” for
I. Liability for remediation and response costs under the Comprehensive
Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act (CERCLA), 42 U.S.C. § 9601
et seq. and other laws;
II. Expenses, such as prepaid rent under the Lease Agreement, incurred in reasonable
reliance upon the representations in the Agreement;
III. Lost opportunity by virtue of being constrained, if not prohibited, from exercising
the option to purchase contained in the Lease as a result of the Hazardous Materials
located on the Option Real Estate;
IV. Purchaser’s attorneys’ fees incurred and to be incurred and necessitated by the
Fred Cuppy incorporated Electro Seal Corporation (Business ID 197405-492) on May 24, 1974 and merged it into
Dynamic Alliance on November 26, 1990 (File # 949241).
Robert Dragani incorporated Northern Acquisition Corporation (Business ID 1990070580) on July 17, 1990. On
March 8, 1991, Robert Dragani amended the Articles of Incorporation to change the company’s name to Electro
Seal Corporation (File # 1694620). At no time did the two (2) Electro Seal Corporations exist simultaneously.
Robert Dragani merged Electro Seal into Northern Indiana Manufacturing, Inc. (Business ID 198207-724) on
December 31, 2008.
IDEM’s counsel requested that the ELJ take judicial notice of the two records showing that Fred Cuppy’s Electro
Seals merged into Dynamic and the other merged into Northern. The ELJ takes official notice pursuant to IC § 4-
21.5-3-26(f)(1).
4 CO, pp.1 – 2.
5 Id.
6 VFC No. 80583069, pp. 2 – 9.
7Id., pp. 1 – 10. -
8 Id., p. 9.
9 Id., p. 11.
2
2024 OEA 001, page 003

Hazardous Materials found on the Option Real Estate; and
V. Incidental and consequential damages due to the results of a Phase II Assessment.10
Northern informed Dynamic that a limited Phase II had detected hazardous substances in
the soil and groundwater and “given the limited scope of the Phase II assessment, the
possibility of other areas of contamination cannot be precluded” and “other areas of
contamination are likely.”11
6. In December 1991, Dynamic hired Environmental Restoration Systems (ERS) and Fred
Krikau & Associates (Krikau) to conduct a site investigation to identify the nature and extent of
impacts from chlorinated solvents at the Site.12
7. On January 31, 1992, ERS submitted a Work Plan on behalf of Dynamic and Northern to
IDEM to address the discovery of PCE in the soil and groundwater at the Site.13 IDEM received
the Work Plan on February 5, 199214 which was the first time15 IDEM learned of the PCE spill
that occurred during the delivery of a drum containing PCE in 1978.
8. On February 13, 1992 IDEM responded to ERS in part, stating:
Thank you for notifying the IDEM of your intention to clean up contamination
discovered on your property. Unfortunately, limited staff resources prevent IDEM from
conducting the comprehensive review necessary to issue a formal approval of your
cleanup. Formal approval can only be granted when the responsible party enters into a
legally binding and enforceable agreement (i.e., a Consent Decree or Agreed Order) with
IDEM. IDEM, therefore, will not be able to review the site characterization and/or
approve the corrective action work plan for this site.16 (emphasis added).
Notwithstanding the lack of a Consent Decree or Agreed Order, IDEM encouraged the
remediation and set forth specific items that should be included in an initial site
characterization and corrective action work plan. IDEM requested that any remediation
documentation be provided to IDEM upon completion that a copy of the documentation be
retained to document the work. IDEM stated, “[t]his of course does not approve your cleanup
nor does it certify that the site is free of contamination. Additional work may be warranted.”17
9. On March 25, 1992, Northern’s counsel sent Dynamic a letter recapping the content of
10 Id., pp. 17 – 19.
11 Id. p. 19
12 Id., pp. 21 - 73.
13 Id. pp. 74 - 81; VFC No. 44914100.
14 VFC No. 44914414. On February 5, 1992, IDEM received a second communication from Dynamic that contained
the exhibits to the Work Plan inadvertently not included in the January 31, 1992 Work Plan.
15 VFC No. 80583069, p.
16 VFC No. 80583069, pp. 82 – 84.
17 Id.
3
2024 OEA 001, page 004

Mittelhauser Corporation’s Phase II Assessment Report, ERS’ Environmental Assessment
Report, ERS’ Corrective Action Plan and IDEM’s response to ERS’ Corrective Action Plan.18
Northern’s counsel informed Dynamic that the proposed cleanup plan submitted by ERS to
IDEM was lacking in certain aspects, the PCE found in the groundwater exceeded maximum
contaminant levels and suggested a “more comprehensive work plan is warranted.”19 Counsel
stated, “given the limited scope of the Phase II assessment, the possibility of other areas of
contamination cannot be precluded.”20 Northern’s counsel emphasized that “without a full and
complete clean-up [Northern] will be unable to exercise its option to purchase under the Lease
and may be required by its lenders to vacate the premises.”21
10. On July 24, 1992, Dynamic wrote Northern and stated, “As you know, we have removed
all of the contaminated soil and we are at this point completed except for determining whether
we can get a no action letter from the state or whether we are going to have to do some
residual pump.”22 Northern did not designate evidence to verify the removal of all of the soil.
11. Between March 25, 1992 and August 31, 1992, Northern and Dynamic and/or their
representatives corresponded to discuss whether additional investigation and/or remediation
would be required for IDEM to “sign off” that all response actions had been completed.23 None
of the designated documents upon which Northern relies in support of its Motion reflects that
the parties discussed whether IDEM could approve the cleanup or certify the Site free of
contamination in the absence of a Consent Decree or Agreed Order.
12. On August 31, 1992, Dynamic wrote Northern and stated environmental consultant
Krikau informed Dynamic
. . . as to the 1, 2 – dichlorobenzene that [sic] there is nothing to be done as there is
nothing in the law that requires that to be removed. As to the contamination of the
groundwater at the northeast part of the property that is the groundwater issue, and as
I understand, the only issue remaining. . . In any event, I am sure we will be able to work
out the remaining issue and we will extend the lease if necessary until the issue is
resolved. [Our consultant] said the levels are so low that it would probably take no
longer than a year or two at the max to clean up any residual groundwater problem but
that in the past, IDEM has signed off for projects that have residual groundwater at
levels higher than we have at present.24 (emphasis added).
18 Through IDEM’s correspondence with ERS in March, 1992, Northern knew that in the absence of a Consent
Decree or Agreed Order, IDEM would not be able to review the site characterization or approve the Corrective
Action Plan.
19 VFC No. 80583069, pp. 85 – 86.
20 Id.
21 Id.
22 Id. p. 96. Neither Dynamic nor Northern entered into a consent decree or agreed order and thus would not be
able to obtain a No Further Action Letter.
23 Id. pp. 85 – 106.
24 Id. pp. 105 - 106.
4
2024 OEA 001, page 005

Northern did not designate evidence supporting Fred Cappy’s statements or its investigation
into Dynamic’s interpretation of Krikau’s statements.
13. On November 18, 1993, Dynamic sent Northern a letter claiming Krikau informed it
There is really nothing further for us to do and as I understand it, there is no
requirement by law for me to do anything further. If we attempt to do anything else it
could jeopardize both of our positions by allowing seepage material into our site which
is not present at this time due to the fact that we have testing samples that indicate the
site is literally free of any hazardous substances or at least ‘legally clean.’
In addition, [the consultant] has checked with IDEM and they are not going to do
anything further about the matter. . . I am still proceeding against UNIVAR to recoup the
money that we have expended and at the least, I am going to attempt to obtain a
judgment that they are liable for any future cleanup. That way[,] you are doubly
protected in the sense that we will have UNIVAR and Dynamic Alliance and myself to
cover you in the event that anyone would require any further cleanup which we know
will not be the case in light of IDEM’s view that they are not interested.25
Northern did not proffer documentary evidence to confirm Dynamic’s claims regarding Krikau’s
statements or Krikau’s conversations with IDEM.
14. In April 1996, Northern hired August Mack Environmental, Inc. (August Mack) to review
the environmental conditions at the Site.26 In its June 19, 1996 Report, August Mack stated in
relevant part,
. . . In April 1991, Northern Acquisition Corp.[27] hired Mittlehauser to conduct a Phase II
environmental assessment . . . The results of the investigation indicated that soil and
groundwater quality impacts were present at the site. Of particular concern were
elevated levels of PCE detected in soil and groundwater and elevated levels of 1,2-
dichlorobenzene detected in soil.[28] . . .
In response to the Phase II results, [Dynamic] retained ERS to develop and implement a
remediation plan for the site. The remedial strategy involved soil excavation and
disposal and groundwater recovery and disposal. It is our understanding that IDEM has
not been contacted and/or involved in the work conducted at the site to date, and that
the work at the site had ceased to await application and acceptance into the IDEM
Voluntary Remediation Program (VRP). Based on our understanding, the site was never
25 Id. p. 131.
26 Id. pp. 148 - 149.
27 It is unclear why August Mack’s report states that Northern Acquisition Corp. hired Mittlehauser in April 1991
when Northern Acquisition Corp. became Electro Seal in March, 1991.
28 Id.
5
2024 OEA 001, page 006

entered into the program.[29] . . .
Groundwater recovery was conducted at the site by pumping groundwater from an
onsite recovery well into tanker trucks. It was reported that approximately 5,000 gallons
of impacted water was recovered. Based on our review of the available information, it
appears that no groundwater was recovered after June 1992.[30]
During groundwater remediation activities, groundwater sampling and analysis was
conducted to monitor the concentrations of contaminants. The target list of parameters
included trichloroethene (TCE), PCE and its breakdown products. PCE, TCE and total 1, 2-
dichloroethene were detected in groundwater samples collected from monitor wells at
the site. . . . These levels [found] exceed the IDEM VRP Tier II cleanup levels.31
No groundwater samples have been collected and/or analyzed since 1993. Sample
analysis results for the 1993 samples indicated that groundwater impacts were present
at the site above the Tier II cleanup levels for PCE. Based upon this information,
groundwater impacts remain at the site and additional work (i.e., sampling and analysis
and/or remedial action) is warranted regarding groundwater at the site. At a minimum,
we recommend groundwater samples be collected to determine the current
groundwater conditions.32
(emphasis added).

4. The parties have moved for summary judgment. The Court may enter judgment for a
party if it finds that “the designated evidentiary matter shows that there is no genuine issue as
to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” Ind.
Tr. R. 56(C); IC § 4-21.5-3-23. The moving party bears the burden of establishing that summary
judgment is appropriate. All facts and inferences must be construed in favor of the non-movant,
and all doubts as to the existence of a material issue must be resolved against the moving
party. Gibson v. Evansville Vanderburgh Building Commission, et al., 725 N.E.2d 949 (Ind. Ct.
App. 2000); City of North Vernon v. Jennings Northwest Regional Utilities, 829 N.E.2d 1, (Ind.
2005); Tibbs v. Huber, Hunt & Nichols, Inc., 668 N.E.2d 248, 249 (Ind. 1996).
A party opposing summary judgment must present specific facts demonstrating a genuine
issue for trial. Hale v. Community Hospitals of Indianapolis, 567 N.E.2d 842, 843 (Ind. Ct. App.
1991) (citing Elkhart Community School Corp. v. Mills, 546 N.E.2d 854 (Ind. Ct. App. 1989)).
“When a motion for summary judgment is made and supported as provided in this rule, an
adverse party may not rest upon the mere allegations or denials of his pleading, but his
response, by affidavits or as otherwise provided in this rule, must set forth specific facts
showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. If he does not so respond, summary judgment, if
appropriate, shall be entered against him.” Ind. Tr. R. 56(E).
An opposing party’s mere assertions, opinions or conclusions of law will not suffice to
create a genuine issue of material fact as to preclude summary judgment. Sanchez v. Hamara,
534 N.E.2d 756, 758 (Ind. Ct. App. 1989), trans. denied; McMahan v. Snap-On Tool Corp., 478
N.E.2d 116, 122 (Ind. Ct. App. 1985). Factual disputes that are irrelevant or unnecessary will not
be considered. Owen v. Vaughn, 479 N.E.2d 83, 87 (Ind. Ct. App. 1985). Once a moving party
sets out a prima facie case in support of the summary judgment, the burden shifts to the non-
movant to establish a factual issue. However, Ind. Tr. R. 56(C) states: “Summary judgment shall
not be granted as of course because the opposing party fails to offer opposing affidavits or
evidence, but the court shall make its determination from the evidentiary matter designated to
the court.”

the current or former owners from their responsibilities to the Site. They did not state that
investigation at the Site was unnecessary.
Here, IDEM
• engaged in a telephone call with Northern requesting an update on the status of the
remedial activities proposed in the ERS Work Plan;
• sent Northern an Information Update Request letter;
• sent Northern a Notice of Liability and Information Request letter;
• sent Northern a Demand for Compliance letter;
• conducted a Site visit to review pertinent documents in Northern’s possession;
• sent Northern an email to inform that IDEM had begun the process to issue the CO;
• sent Northern an email to provide a description of the investigation IDEM was
requesting;
• sent Northern an email after Northern didn’t follow-up its own email stating it would
“take care of this matter”; and
• issued Northern a Demand for Compliance letter with an attached Agreed Order.
In short, the agency did not change its position so as to cause prejudice to Northern.
Richmond State Hosp. v. Brattain, 961 N.E.2d 1010, 1012 (Ind. 2012) (quoting Shafer v. Lambie,
667 N.E.2d 226, 231 (Ind. Ct. App. 1996)). Northern’s mere assertions that it reasonably
believed any liability for the PCE spill resided with Dynamic and IDEM only shifted its focus after
Dynamic informed the agency it did not have the money are not supported by IDEM’s actions.
IDEM neither misled Northern into believing its continued lack of responsiveness in addressing
the contamination at the Site was permissible nor engaged in affirmative misconduct by not
asking Northern to do what it promised to do. Given the fact that Dalton is an unpublished
case, and the facts differ significantly from the Cause at hand, the Court does not find it
persuasive.81
15. Northern argues it “has been prejudiced by IDEM’s delay in pursuing the actual polluter
which now claims to be unable to pay for a cleanup”82 but its argument is self-serving and
unconvincing. Notwithstanding the fact that Northern was aware of what was and was not
happening at the Site with respect to investigation and remediation, it still chose to purchase
81 Unpublished trial court decisions do not serve as precedent and may only be considered for their persuasive
value. See Ind. Dep’t of Natural Res. V. United Minerals, Inc., 686 N.E.2d 851, 857 (Ind. Ct. App. 1997), trans.
denied.
82 Northern Brief, p. 8.
18
2024 OEA 001, page 019

the property in July 1996.83 To date, it continues to use the Site and yet has not addressed the
issues it raised to Dynamic after Northern started leasing in 1991. Northern cannot complain it
has been prejudiced by its perceived “IDEM’s delay” when Northern repeatedly and
consistently failed to take action for the same issues for which it is now being held accountable.
Clearly, an adequate groundwater investigation of a hazardous substance release is in the
public interest, and the public’s interest in having that information to address outstanding risks
outweighs Northern’s unsupported belief that, as a responsible person, it has been prejudiced.
The remaining four claims appearing in Northern’s Petition were neither argued in any of its
subsequent pleadings nor supported by any documentary evidence.
Northern raised four issues in its Petition84 without addressing any of them in its Motion for
Summary Judgment, Brief in Support, Reply or at Oral Argument:
I. Whether the claims against Northern are arbitrary, capricious, and an abuse of
discretion;
II. Whether the [CO] is void for vagueness under Indiana law;
III. Whether the vagueness of the [CO] violates due process and due course of law rights
under the U.S. Constitution and Indiana Constitution; and
IV. Whether the [CO] or IDEM’s implementation of the [CO] violates . . . [IC § 4-21.5] or
other Indiana law.
Pursuant to Ind. Tr. R. 56 (E) “an adverse party may not rest upon the mere allegations or
denials of his pleading, but his response, by affidavits or as otherwise provided in this rule, must
set forth specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. If he does not so respond,
summary judgment, if appropriate, shall be entered against him.” A party’s mere assertions,
opinions or conclusions of law will not suffice to create a genuine issue of material fact as to
preclude summary judgment. Sanchez, supra at 758; McMahan, supra at 122.
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED Northern’s Motion for Summary
Judgment is DENIED, and IDEM’s Motion for Summary Judgment is GRANTED. This case is
DISMISSED. All further proceedings are VACATED.
You are hereby further notified that pursuant to provisions of IC § 4-21.5-7-5, the Office of
Environmental Adjudication serves as the Ultimate Authority in the administrative review of
decisions of the Commissioner of the Indiana Department of Environmental Management. This
is a Final Order subject to Judicial Review consistent with applicable provisions of IC § 4-21.5.
Pursuant to IC § 4-21.5-5-5, a Petition for Judicial Review of this Final Order is timely only if it is
filed with a civil court of competent jurisdiction within thirty (30) days after the date this notice

84 Petition, pp. 2 – 3.
19
2024 OEA 001, page 020

is served.
IT IS SO ORDERED this 31st day of January, 2024 in Indianapolis, IN.
